paragraphs: First: his denial of reflection upon the intelligible (al-naẓar fī al-maʿqūl), and his censure of its practitioners. This is recorded in more than one place of his books. Also: that he does not affirm the angels in the way the Children of Israel affirm them — as living forms, knowing, present, [sent] on missions, in the manner in which the prophets were dispatched. Rather, he claimed that this name — I mean our saying "angel" and "angels" — applies only to the bodies through which God works His acts, such as fire, clouds, winds, and the like. Another statement is reported of him in this, which I shall mention elsewhere, and I shall mention the answer to him.

Also: he forbids the blood of fish, and permits of the locust only the four kinds mentioned by their names. He forbade intercourse by night, lest the [morning] prayer escape a man. He made obligatory the impurity [contracted] from the earth in this age. It is reported of him that he used to say: the obligations are binding only upon one twenty years old. He forbade on the Sabbath [certain] things, such as washing the hand with ushnān (soapwort), and the like. He forbade the lamp on the festival eve — in the manner the majority do on the Sabbath eve. He claimed that the saying of Scripture [Lev 1:15] "וְהִקְרִיב הַכֹּהֵן… וּמָלַק אֶת רֹאשׁוֹ" is an act [performed] after the slaughter. It is reported of him that he used to permit the testimony of the Muslims regarding the sighting of the new moon.

These, then, are the substance of the statements of those who have appeared down to this age, so far as has reached us. Some of these sects have already lapsed — such as the Maghāriyya, the Sadducees, and likewise the adherents of "Ismaʿīl al-ʿUkbarī," of whom no one remains; nor is there anyone who submits to reflection in this age who inclines to his statement. As for the ʿAnaniyya — they have dwindled greatly, until there came to them one who came in [their] diminishing. As for the adherents of "Abū ʿĪsā al-Iṣfahānī" — what remains of them, in Damascus alone, is like twenty souls. As for the Yudghanites — there is of them a small remnant in Iṣfahān. But dissension has multiplied greatly in this age among our own people; and we shall set out the dissension that is among them in [matters of] principle — so that we may not leave anything that needs treatment unmentioned.
: Daniel al-Qūmisī held a restricted rationalist theology: the angels are not personal beings but natural phenomena (fire, wind, clouds).
: The laws of the locust — Lev 11:22 specifies four kinds; Daniel limits the permission to these four, where others took a broader view.
: A radical view: that the obligations bind only one past the age of twenty.
: Arabic al-ushnān, soapwort; washing with it on the Sabbath is forbidden, per Daniel.
: Meliqah after slaughter — a view Q regards as mistaken, meliqah being a separate rite for a bird-offering (Lev 1:15), not an act following ordinary slaughter.

: The state of the sects per Q in 937 CE: the Sadducees, Maghāriyya, and ʿUkbarīs extinct; the ʿAnanites dwindling; the Yudghanites a remnant in Iṣfahān; the ʿĪsawiyya some twenty souls in Damascus; the Karaites fragmenting — a sober, realistic picture of tenth-century Jewish sectarianism.
